scenes.visual: chain pumps, synthase spends; a leak lets protons bypass the synthase
scenes.narration: Picture the electron transport chain and ATP synthase as a couple in a committed relationship. Normally they are tightly coupled. The chain builds the proton gradient, and ATP synthase spends it to make ATP. Uncoupling is the breakup. Protons find another way back across the membrane instead of going through ATP synthase, so the energy of the gradient is released as heat rather than captured as ATP. The chain keeps pumping furiously, oxygen consumption climbs, but the partnership no longer produces anything useful.
scenes.slideTitle: Uncoupling: When the Mitochondrial Romance Ends
scenes.notes: Picture the electron-transport chain and ATP synthase as a couple in a committed relationship. Normally they are tightly coupled: the chain builds the proton gradient, and ATP synthase spends it to make ATP. Uncoupling is the breakup. Protons find another way back across the membrane instead of going through ATP synthase, so the energy of the gradient is released as heat rather than captured as ATP. The chain keeps pumping furiously, oxygen consumption climbs, but the partnership no longer produces anything useful. Hold onto this image, because we will return to it for thermogenesis, brown fat, and drugs that deliberately cause the split.

scenes.visual: three agents, three readouts, built row by row
scenes.narration: This table forces you to reason like the chain itself. An ETC inhibitor, such as rotenone or cyanide, shuts everything down. Oxygen consumption, ATP synthesis and the proton gradient all fall. An ATP synthase inhibitor, oligomycin, blocks the exit for protons, so synthesis falls and consumption falls, but the gradient backs up and rises. The uncoupler is the counterintuitive case. ATP synthesis falls and the gradient collapses, yet oxygen consumption increases. Why? Because with the gradient leaking away, the chain races to rebuild it, pumping faster and burning more oxygen. If you can predict each row, you understand how coupling actually works.

scenes.visual: O2 trace jumps when ADP is added
scenes.narration: Electrons refuse to flow through the transport chain unless ADP is available to be turned into ATP. Watch the oxygen consumption trace, respiration idles until ADP is added, then the rate jumps, and it falls again once the supply of ADP is nearly exhausted. This is acceptor control, also called respiratory control, and it is the cell's way of matching fuel burning to demand. ADP is the signal for need. When the cell has spent its ATP, the ADP it generates lifts the brake on the chain. This is a clean example of metabolism being governed by energy charge rather than by substrate alone.

scenes.visual: ATP synthase runs backward in hypoxia; IF1 brake
scenes.narration: ATP synthase is reversible. During normal respiration, the proton gradient drives it forward to make ATP. But in ischemia or severe hypoxia, oxygen runs low, the chain stalls, and the gradient collapses. Now the enzyme can spin backward, hydrolyzing the cell's remaining ATP in a futile attempt to rebuild the gradient, wasting precious energy exactly when it is scarcest. The inhibitory factor IF1 is the emergency brake. It binds at low pH, which marks oxygen deprivation, and blocks the reverse rotation, protecting cellular ATP.
scenes.slideTitle: Clinical Insight: IF1 and Reverse Mode
scenes.notes: ATP synthase is reversible. During normal respiration the proton gradient drives it forward to make ATP. But in ischemia or severe hypoxia, oxygen runs low, the chain stalls, and the gradient collapses. Now the enzyme can spin backward, hydrolyzing the cell's remaining ATP in a futile attempt to rebuild the gradient, wasting precious energy exactly when it is scarcest. The inhibitory factor IF1 is the emergency brake. It binds at low pH, which marks oxygen deprivation, and blocks the reverse rotation, protecting cellular ATP. Note also that IF1 is overexpressed in some cancers, where it may help drive the shift toward aerobic glycolysis.
